In brief

As the day's light dies away in Nausicaa and "far away the lights of the lighthouses" shine forth, Gerty thinks that "soon the lamplighter would be going his rounds past the presbyterian church grounds and along by shady Tritonville avenue where the couples walked and lighting the lamp near her window where Reggy Wylie used to turn his freewheel like she read in that book The Lamplighter by Miss Cummins, author of Mabel Vaughan and other tales." This novel by American writer Maria Cummins gave Joyce many ideas for his chapter: the name of his protagonist, the name of the boy she wants to marry, the girl's nasty temper, her religious piety, and her desire to rise above her humble surroundings. But he made something very different from the materials at hand.

At more length

First published in 1854, The Lamplighter proved immensely popular: in the first five months it sold more than 65,000 copies, and there were numerous subsequent editions as well as overseas translations. At the beginning of the story eight-year-old Gerty Flint is an impoverished orphan living with her drunken, neglectful, punitive guardian Nan Grant in the slums of Boston. She is unloved, uneducated, untrusted with formative responsibilities, badly clothed, and verbally abused so often that she joins others in thinking herself wicked. A kind old lamplighter named Trueman Flint rescues the child by taking her into his poor home, where she is befriended by a neighbor boy named Willie. The boy is bright and hardworking, and when he is apprenticed to an apothecary he sets his sights on rising in the world and becoming as prosperous as the people he sees in nice houses. By the end of the novel he has succeeded in this aim and has married Gerty. For both characters The Lamplighter is a rags-to-riches story.

Not coincidentally, it is also a story of moral improvement. Gerty is a wellmeaning child, but early in their life together True hears her "uttering the most bitter invectives against Nan Grant. The child's language expressed unmitigated hatred, and even a hope of future revenge.... True's own disposition was so amiable and forgiving, that he could not imagine that anyone, and especially a little child, should long retain feelings of anger and bitterness. Gerty had shown herself so mild and patient since she had been with him, that it had never occurred to him to dread any difficulty in the management of the child. Now, however, as he observed her flashing eyes, and noticed the doubling of her little fist as she menaced Nan with her future wrath, he had an undefined, half-formed presentiment of coming trouble in the control of his little charge.... He saw in her something which needed a check, and felt himself unfit to apply it." As for her young friend, "Willie tried once or twice to stop the current of her abusive language; but soon desisted, for she did not pay the least attention to him. He could not help smiling at her childish wrath, nor could he resist sympathising with her in a degree. But he was conscious that Gerty was exhibiting a very hot temper, and began to understand what made everybody think her so bad" (ch. 5).

Gerty is saved from herself by becoming a Good Christian. A plaster figurine of a praying boy introduces her to the notion of self-improvement through prayer. Willie's mother teaches her housekeeping. A blind woman named Emily Graham teaches her to forgive. When True dies, and she moves in with Emily, and Emily's jealous housekeeper destroys her precious mementoes of True, she overcomes her rage through prayer. She leaves Emily's house to take care of Willie's terminally ill mother. She meets a desperately ill Nan Grant and forgives her. And so forth. Through the course of many hardships and trials, the young woman now called Gertrude proves a model of "self-denial," "self-command," "self-control," "self-sacrifice," and "self-possession." Eventually Willie and Gertrude marry and settle into happy domesticity. In the novel's final chapter they gaze out the window of their comfortable house at their old street, sadly contemplating the past as a newfangled "gasman" lights the lamps. Gertrude says that Uncle True's "lamp still burns brightly in heaven, Willie; and its light is not yet gone out on earth!" (ch. 48).

Joyce's Gerty (aka Gertrude) MacDowell is fully as pious as Gerty Flint, but as an Irish Catholic her piety takes the form of devotion to the Blessed Virgin. Mary's iconographic color, blue, pervades the first half of Nausicaa and her attributes fill both Gerty's thoughts and the prayers wafting out of the church named for Mary, Star of the Sea. But Gerty also displays an unchristian tendency to judge other people harshly. Edy Boardman, who is inclined to make fun of her (pure jealousy, in Gerty's view), is "squinty Edy," an "Irritable little gnat," "Miss puny little Edy." She prides herself on being "very petite but she never had a foot like Gerty MacDowell, a five." The highspirited and humorous Cissy Caffrey offers no offense but still comes in for some scorn. Gerty watches her "tossing her hair behind her which had a good enough colour if there had been more of it." Energetically wrangling two small boys on the sand, she becomes unladylike, "the flimsy blouse she bought only a fortnight before like a rag on her back and a bit of her petticoat hanging like a caricature." Nor does Gerty feel tender toward the "squalling baby" and "exasperating little brats of twins." The boys are "Little monkeys common as ditchwater. Someone ought to take them and give them a good hiding for themselves to keep them in their places, the both of them." (She shares this tendency with Nan Grant.)

The rags-to-riches trope also plays a part in Gerty's mentality. She comes from a lower-middle-class family where money is tight, but she dresses as elegantly as possible and considers herself born for better things: "Had kind fate but willed her to be born a gentlewoman of high degree in her own right and had she only received the benefit of a good education Gerty MacDowell might easily have held her own beside any lady in the land and have seen herself exquisitely gowned with jewels on her brow and patrician suitors at her feet vying with one another to pay their devoirs to her." Her hopes rest on marrying her childhood love Reggy Wylie, whose family is Protestant and better-off, and she imagines how she will be regarded when they are married: "in the fashionable intelligence Mrs Gertrude Wylie was wearing a sumptuous confection of grey trimmed with expensive blue fox." Gerty's sense of innate aristocracy is not unrelated to her tendency to look down on the people around her as unbeautiful and "common."

As much as he borrows from Cummins, Joyce uses his found materials to construct a quite different character and story. Gerty's piety has not yet resulted in much Christian self-improvement. She is a dutiful daughter and hopes to become a devoted wife, but she thinks less of honing her housekeeping skills than of making herself attractive. Unlike Gerty Flint, she displays a real flair for heterosexual flirtation and an awareness of her sexual power. The grim narrative logic of Cummins's tale—repress your unruly feelings, cultivate a life of self-sacrificing service, and you will be rewarded with marriage and money—is absent from Joyce's. He offers a more unfair sort of grimness: an accident has rendered the heroine lame and hence, it seems, unmarriageable. But he also leaves room for joy. The masturbatory interaction on the beach is not a dismally inhuman thing but a portal of discovery—a first taste of sexual self-discovery for Gerty and a restorative sexual release for Bloom. Nausicaa, like A Portrait of the Artist, shows the energy of religious devotion being turned away from clerical sexual repression and relocated in profane love.

Many Joyceans seem to believe that the prose style of Nausicaa is a mocking parody of The Lamplighter. It is not: Cummins writes in a plain, straightforward style that has almost nothing in common with Joyce's labored preciosity. It can hardly be doubted that his purple prose constitutes an invitation to mockery, and he may possibly have shared the opinion expressed by Nathaniel Hawthorne in an 1855 letter: "What is the mystery of these innumerable editions of The Lamplighter, and other books neither better nor worse?... America is now wholly given over to a d—d mob of scribbling women." But even if Joyce imitated the style of certain sentimental female writers (I do not know which ones they might be), his thirteenth chapter is something more than a mere send-up. Many of its romantic flourishes resemble verbal constructions found in his own letters and in A Portrait of the Artist. Silly romantic Gerty MacDowell is in part a stylized projection of silly romantic Jim Joyce.

John Hunt 2026
